searchText: Has there been any serious study in removing altogether optimistic sync? As in allowing validators to be completely optimistic (but not allowing them to propose through an external builder). I understand there are some risks of validators being fed an invalid chain or a bug leading to many validators syncing at the same time compounds other bugs, but one of our biggest complexities lie in how we deal with optimistic sync and I can't help but feel that bugs arising from that complexity are more harmful cc <@291925846556540928> Is there a reason contract addresses aren’t just the hash of the bytecode? Seems like it would save space and make finding contract addresses easier You mapreduce the contract to save the contract code once and move the state somewhere else so people can have multiple instances of it (Reposted from execution — wasn’t sure where to write this)

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: Has there been any serious study in removing altogether optimistic sync? As in allowing validators to be completely optimistic (but not allowing them to propose through an external builder). I understand there are some risks of validators being fed an invalid chain or a bug leading to many validators syncing at the same time compounds other bugs, but one of our biggest complexities lie in how we deal with optimistic sync and I can't help but feel that bugs arising from that complexity are more harmful

excerpts.author: maxandrew
excerpts.content: Is there a reason contract addresses aren’t just the hash of the bytecode? Seems like it would save space and make finding contract addresses easier

excerpts.author: maxandrew
excerpts.content: You mapreduce the contract to save the contract code once and move the state somewhere else so people can have multiple instances of it
